name: Wright's Law
statement: Every time cumulative production doubles, the cost per unit falls by a constant percentage.
statementAccent: the cost per unit falls by a constant percentage
meaning: For every doubling of the total number of units ever produced, the cost or labour per unit drops by a roughly fixed percentage. Cost declines track accumulated production experience, not calendar time. Plotting unit cost against cumulative output on log-log axes yields an approximately straight downward line.
mechanism: The drivers are learning by doing, process and product redesign, standardisation and tooling, and economies of scale — workers and organisations get faster and waste less as they repeat a task, and the product and its production are refined. A learning rate of, say, twenty percent means each cumulative doubling brings costs to about eighty percent of their prior level, the so-called eighty-percent curve. A caveat runs through the mechanism: these forces are entangled with scale, research spending, and time, and are hard to separate cleanly.

examples.text: Wright's original 1936 study of airframe manufacturing found that labour per plane fell by a roughly constant fraction with each doubling of cumulative output — the founding empirical case.

Solar module prices fall by roughly a fifth per doubling of cumulative shipments — a solar-specific instance sometimes called Swanson's law — carrying prices from over a hundred dollars a watt in the 1970s to a fraction of a dollar today.
A 2013 study of sixty-two technologies found Wright's law produced the best cost forecasts, with time-based Moore's law close behind because production itself tends to grow exponentially.

variants.name: The BCG experience curve
variants.text: Bruce Henderson's 1960s generalisation at the Boston Consulting Group, covering total costs including overhead and marketing rather than just labour — related but distinct, and typically quoted at a steeper rate per doubling.

variants.name: Moore's law
variants.text: The contrast case: Moore's law is a function of time, with transistor counts doubling every couple of years, whereas Wright's law is a function of cumulative production; the two coincide only when output grows exponentially.

whyItMatters: It is one of the most useful regularities in technology forecasting and industrial strategy, letting analysts project how costs fall as a technology scales. It has proved a strong predictor across dozens of industries, from aircraft to solar to semiconductors, and underlies the case that scaling up production is itself a route to lower cost.

working.text: to project a technology's future cost, extrapolate the constant percentage fall per doubling of total units produced.
tie cost declines to how much has been made, not how much time has passed, since production experience is the driver.
estimate the learning rate from the sector's own data rather than assuming a universal figure, and expect it to vary.

limits: It is an empirical regularity, not a physical law: the percentage varies by industry and is not guaranteed to persist. The learning mechanism is entangled with economies of scale, research spending, and time, so experience effects are hard to isolate — some argue they cannot be cleanly separated from scale. Disruptive technology shifts, raw-material cost floors, saturated learning, or supply shocks can bend or break the curve. Even the best forecasting models carry errors that grow over the horizon. It is best treated as an empirically grounded regularity rather than a guaranteed causal law.
misreadings: It is not the same as the Boston Consulting Group's experience curve, which covers total costs and came decades later, nor as Moore's law, which runs on time rather than cumulative production. And the constant percentage is a robust pattern, not a law of nature that must hold at a fixed rate forever.
origin: Stated by the aeronautical engineer Theodore Paul Wright in 'Factors Affecting the Cost of Airplanes,' Journal of the Aeronautical Sciences 3(4):122-128 (1936), from data on aircraft manufacturing.

sources.text: Experience curve effect, Wikipedia. — Wright's 1936 origin, the learning-rate convention, and the distinction from the BCG experience curve.
Nagy, Farmer, Bui & Trancik, "Statistical Basis for Predicting Technological Progress," PLOS ONE (2013). — the sixty-two-technology comparison of Wright's law and Moore's law.
